---
title: "Use the viewer"
guide-section: How-to guides
---

Press `?` in the viewer for every key and mouse action.

## Move around

The wheel zooms (with Shift time only, with Ctrl distance only), and the arrows pan. In the pan tool a drag moves the view; in any tool the middle button, or Space and drag, does. Tab moves on by a screen in time, and Shift+Tab back. Both skip gaps in the recording: the view stops where the data ends, so the screen stays full of it, and the next press goes to where it starts again. The strip under the time axis is the whole recording: click or drag on it to move the window, and press `b` to go back to the view before a jump. `w` fits the whole recording.

## Set the colours

The colour bar's axis spans the values on screen. Drag a triangle to move that limit, or the part between them to move both; the axis stays put. A click elsewhere on the bar, or `a`, sets the limits from what is on screen, leaving out the extreme 1 % at each end. The cog (top right, or `p`) opens the menu: its Display tab picks the scale (log10 by default), the limits and the colour map.

## Measure

The ruler (`m`) measures between two clicks: the difference along each axis and the slope, a speed when x is time. A third click starts again; Esc clears it, then returns to pan.

## Annotate

Sign in first with the button at the top right, if the server asks you to: on a trusting server, pick your name or type a new one.

1. Pick a tool: `1` point, `2` path, `3` polygon, `4` box.
2. Click to place points. End a path or polygon with Enter, a double-click or a right-click.
3. Type a label in the box that opens, or press Enter to keep the last one.

Drawings go into the set being edited and are saved as you go; the dot beside your name is filled once they are. The cog menu's Annotations tab lists the sets. Rest the mouse on an annotation, or on a counted group, for a summary of it. With thousands of a set's annotations on screen, the set is shaded by how many cover each pixel; zoom in to see them one by one. To edit, switch to the select tool (`v`, or double-click): drag an annotation or a vertex to move it, double-click a side to add a vertex, and press Delete to remove.

## Correct someone else's annotations

Select them and press `c` to copy them into your own set. Each copy records where it came from in `derived_from` and `derived_revision`. Only a set's owner can change it.

## Move sets between the viewer and DASCore

"download" gives the set being edited as a zip of its folder. "load" makes a new set from such a zip, or from a table of annotations (`.parquet` or `.csv`).

## Download an area

1. In the cog menu's Download tab, take an area: from the selected annotation, from the window on screen, or by dragging a box (`d`).
2. Tick the products to take (the raw data, where there is some, unless you choose otherwise); it shows their size.
3. Press download for one DASDAE file, or Sync (under `dastor browse --data-dir`) to write it into your local data directory.

A synced file is named for the recording, the product and the start of the area, with a number added if that name is taken, so nothing is replaced. The directory's spool sees it when it next indexes (`spool.update()`).

## See where the fibre lies

When the data directory holds a DASCore inventory (`.inventory`) and the recordings carry its acquisition keys, the map button in the top bar opens a map to the left of the data; on a wide window it is open from the start. A recording whose key the inventory lacks is not on the map, and with no recording on it there is no button. It draws the fibre of the recording on show from the inventory; other fibres are thin and grey. The part of the fibre the recording covers is thick, and the stretch on screen is highlighted. The text under the map's title is what the inventory says of the fibre, its array and network, and the recording, including whatever it says about how well the positions are known; click it to read it all. The map draws what the inventory states and knows no more: where positions were inferred and not surveyed, it is the inventory's description which has to say so.

The map and the data are linked. Hovering the data marks the place on the map, and hovering the fibre marks its distance in the data and lists the inventory's labels there. It also gives what the inventory says of that stretch of the geometry, if anything. Where the fibre passes one spot more than once the other distances are listed, and where the inventory states much more fibre than the line drawn is long (a coil, slack, or a route drawn with few points) the stretch is given. Distances are rounded to 10 m on a fibre of kilometres and less on a short one, since a place on a fibre is rarely known better. A click on a fibre shows that place in the data and marks it for a moment, opening a recording which covers it if the one on show does not.

The colour menu paints the fibre with a label group or a measured column of the inventory, with the same colours in a strip beside the data, or with the mean along time of the data on screen.

An inventory in longitude and latitude can have background layers and a web map under it, if the [config](41-config.qmd#map) names them. The web map loads tiles from the internet, so it stays off until its box is ticked; the browser then remembers the tick. An inventory in any other coordinates (a local x, y, z or a projected grid) is drawn as a plane to scale, from its first two axes, with no background.

A window too narrow for the map and the data side by side closes the map until there is room again.

## Choose the levels to zoom through

The pyramid icon at the bottom right (or `l`) opens the levels, in the cog menu's Display tab: one row for each resolution of the recording's [products](31-products.qmd), the coarsest at the top and 1, the finest, at the bottom. Tick the ones to zoom through; where several products share a resolution, pick one, or set every level at once. Level 0 is the raw data, which is loaded only when ticked. The numbers beside the icon show the level on screen; click one to hold the view on it, and "auto" to follow the zoom again.
